concept.name: OAuth2 Authorization Flows

relationships.description: Connects OAuth2 Authorization Flows to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access without sharing user passwords, using distinct grant flows tailored to confidential backends, public SPAs/mobile apps, headless devices, and service-to-service workloads. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flows in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) for any user-facing login and Client Credentials for machine-to-machine calls; never use Implicit or ROPC.

concept.whyItMatters: Exposing user passwords to third-party apps or storing long-lived credentials in browser JavaScript creates catastrophic blast radii. OAuth 2.0 separates authentication (often via OpenID Connect) from scoped, revocable, short-lived access tokens so compromised clients cannot take over an entire account.
whenToUse: Granting third-party or first-party web/mobile apps scoped, revocable access to user resources via `Authorization Code + PKCE`.
Authenticating backend microservices or batch jobs to internal APIs via `Client Credentials` without a human user in the loop.
Authorizing input-constrained devices (smart TVs, CLI tools) via the `Device Authorization Grant` (RFC 8628).
whenNotToUse: Using `Implicit` flow (`response_type=token`) for SPAs; it leaks access tokens in browser URL fragments, history, and Referer headers.
Using `Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC)` to collect raw user passwords in your own login form, bypassing MFA, SSO, and federated IdPs.
Treating an opaque OAuth 2.0 access token as user identity proof; use an OpenID Connect (OIDC) `id_token` or `/userinfo` endpoint for authentication.
keyPoints: PKCE (RFC 7636) binds the authorization request to the token exchange using a per-session `code_verifier` and SHA-256 `code_challenge`, preventing authorization code interception on public and confidential clients alike.
Always validate the `state` parameter (cryptographically random, bound to the user's browser session) on the `/callback` endpoint to block Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) login attacks.
Use short-lived access tokens (5–15 minutes) paired with Refresh Token Rotation (`refresh_token` invalidated on single use) and reuse detection to limit stolen token windows.
For SPAs, the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern keeps `client_secret` and refresh tokens in an HttpOnly, SameSite cookie on a confidential server rather than browser `localStorage`.
Confidential server-to-server workloads use `grant_type=client_credentials` with mTLS or `private_key_jwt` (RFC 7523) instead of static shared secrets.

examples.title: Migrating a React SPA from Implicit Flow to Auth Code + PKCE via BFF
examples.scenario: A SaaS dashboard used `response_type=token` (Implicit flow) and stored 24-hour JWTs in `localStorage`, exposing tokens to any third-party analytics XSS vulnerability.
examples.outcome: Moving token exchange into an API Gateway BFF using Authorization Code + PKCE (`S256`) and issuing `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies eliminated token exposure in browser JS and cut token lifetime to 10 minutes with silent server-side refresh.

examples.title: Headless CLI Authentication with RFC 8628 Device Flow
examples.scenario: A developer CLI tool needed to access a cloud deployment API on SSH-only Linux servers where opening a local browser redirect to `localhost:8080` failed.
examples.outcome: Implementing Device Authorization Grant (`POST /oauth/device/code`) let the CLI display an 8-character `user_code` and verification URL; the developer approved it on their laptop browser while the CLI polled `/oauth/token` every 5 seconds.

tradeOffs.pro: Direct SPA PKCE requires zero session-management backend and works with static CDN hosting.
tradeOffs.con: Tokens reside in browser memory or storage (vulnerable to XSS), whereas a BFF keeps tokens server-side behind `HttpOnly` cookies.

tradeOffs.factor: JWT Access Tokens vs. Opaque Reference Tokens
tradeOffs.pro: Self-contained JWTs allow resource servers to verify signatures (`JWKS`) locally in <1ms without calling the authorization server.
tradeOffs.con: JWTs cannot be immediately revoked before expiration without maintaining a distributed revocation list or short 5-minute TTLs.

tradeOffs.factor: Refresh Token Rotation vs. Static Refresh Tokens
tradeOffs.pro: Rotating refresh tokens on every `/token` call detects replay if either the legitimate client or an attacker reuses an old token, revoking the entire token family.
tradeOffs.con: Concurrent browser tabs racing to refresh the same token can trigger false-positive reuse revocations without a brief 5–10s grace window or single-flight lock.

failureModes.name: Authorization Code Interception
failureModes.description: On mobile or desktop apps with custom URI schemes (`myapp://callback`), a malicious app registers the same scheme and steals the `code` from the redirect.
failureModes.mitigation: Mandate PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) on the authorization server; the attacker cannot exchange the stolen `code` without the original `code_verifier`.

failureModes.name: Open Redirect & Token Leakage
failureModes.description: Wildcard `redirect_uri` matching (e.g., `https://app.example.com/*`) lets an attacker redirect the authorization code to an attacker-controlled open redirect path.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce exact byte-for-byte `redirect_uri` matching in the authorization server configuration; never allow wildcard paths or query-string prefixes.

failureModes.name: CSRF on Callback Endpoint
failureModes.description: An attacker initiates an OAuth flow with their own account and tricks a victim into visiting the attacker's `/callback?code=...` URL, binding the victim's session to the attacker's account.
failureModes.mitigation: Generate a 128-bit random `state` value stored in an `HttpOnly` cookie before redirecting, and reject any callback where `state` is missing or mismatched.

failureModes.name: Confused Deputy / Token Replay Across Audiences
failureModes.description: A resource server accepts a valid JWT issued for a different API because it only checks signature and `exp`, ignoring the `aud` (audience) and `scope` claims.
failureModes.mitigation: Validate `iss`, `aud` (must match the exact resource server identifier), `exp`, and required `scope` on every API request.

commonMistakes: Using `client_secret` inside a mobile app or SPA bundle—public clients cannot keep secrets, so any secret shipped in client code is compromised immediately.
Confusing OAuth 2.0 (authorization) with OpenID Connect (authentication) and skipping `id_token` `nonce` and `aud` validation.
Setting refresh token lifetimes to infinite without idle timeouts or rotation, leaving stolen sessions active for years.
Passing `access_token` in URL query parameters (`?access_token=...`), which leaks credentials into proxy logs, browser history, and Referer headers.
Skipping `PKCE` on confidential web servers—OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE for all Authorization Code flows to close code-injection vectors.

sections.content:
## The idea

OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is a **delegation framework**, not an authentication protocol. It defines four roles: the **Resource Owner** (user), the **Client** (app requesting access), the **Authorization Server** (IdP issuing tokens), and the **Resource Server** (API hosting protected data).

Instead of handing the Client a user's password, the Authorization Server authenticates the user on its own trusted domain, obtains consent for specific `scope` strings (e.g., `orders:read`), and issues a short-lived `access_token` to the Client. The Client presents that token as a Bearer credential (`Authorization: Bearer <token>`) to the Resource Server.

## Concrete walkthrough

Here is the exact **Authorization Code + PKCE** flow for a web or mobile client:

1. **Generate PKCE & State**: The Client generates a 64-byte random `code_verifier`, computes `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))`, and creates a random `state` token bound to the user's session.
2. **Authorization Redirect**: The Client redirects the user's browser to `GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=web-app&redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/cb&scope=openid+profile+orders:read&state=xyz&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256`.
3. **User Auth & Consent**: The Authorization Server authenticates the user (password + WebAuthn/MFA) and redirects back to `redirect_uri?code=auth_9f8a&state=xyz`.
4. **State Verification & Token Exchange**: The Client verifies `state == xyz`, then makes a back-channel `POST /oauth/token` sending `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code=auth_9f8a`, `redirect_uri`, `client_id`, and the raw `code_verifier`.
5. **PKCE Validation & Token Issue**: The Authorization Server hashes `code_verifier`, confirms it matches the stored `code_challenge`, invalidates `auth_9f8a` (single-use), and returns `{access_token (10m), refresh_token (7d), id_token}`.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Choosing the right grant type and OIDC layering
sections.content:
## Choosing the right grant type and OIDC layering

OAuth 2.1 consolidates the specification around four surviving patterns:

- **Authorization Code + PKCE**: Mandatory for all interactive user flows (confidential web backends, SPAs, native mobile).
- **Client Credentials (`grant_type=client_credentials`)**: For service-to-service calls with no user context. Prefer `private_key_jwt` (signed JWT assertion) or mTLS over static `client_secret` strings.
- **Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628)**: For CLI tools, smart TVs, and IoT devices lacking a browser.
- **Refresh Token Grant**: Silent renewal of short-lived access tokens; pair with **DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession, RFC 9449)** when sender-constraining tokens is required.

**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** sits cleanly on top of OAuth 2.0 by adding the `openid` scope, returning a signed JWT `id_token` containing `sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and `nonce` so the Client knows *who* logged in.

## OAuth 2.0 grant flow comparison

| Grant Flow | Client Type | User Involved? | Primary Mechanism | Status in OAuth 2.1 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Auth Code + PKCE** | Confidential & Public | Yes | Temp `code` + SHA-256 `code_verifier` | **Recommended default** |
| **Client Credentials** | Confidential (Backend) | No | `client_id` + `private_key_jwt` / mTLS | **Recommended for M2M** |
| **Device Authorization** | Input-constrained | Yes (2nd device) | `device_code` polling + `user_code` | **Supported (RFC 8628)** |
| **Implicit (`token`)** | Public (Legacy SPA) | Yes | Access token in URL `#fragment` | **Removed / Deprecated** |
| **ROPC (`password`)** | First-party legacy | Yes | Raw username & password to `/token` | **Removed / Deprecated** |

## Failure modes

**1. Missing `aud` Validation in Multi-Tenant APIs**: If Service A and Service B share the same IdP, a token minted for `aud: service-a` with `scope: read` can be replayed against Service B unless Service B explicitly rejects tokens whose `aud` claim does not include `service-b`.

**2. Refresh Token Race Conditions**: In SPAs making 5 parallel API calls when a 10-minute access token expires, all 5 requests may try to use the same single-use `refresh_token`. Request #1 succeeds and rotates the token; Requests #2–#5 trigger reuse detection and revoke the user's entire session.

**3. `alg: none` or Key Confusion Attacks**: Weak JWT libraries that trust the unverified token header's `alg` field can be tricked into accepting unsigned tokens or verifying RS256 public keys as HS256 HMAC secrets.

## Production hardening & token lifecycle

Hardening an OAuth 2.0 deployment requires defense-in-depth across client and server:

- **Pin Algorithms & Keys**: Resource servers should hardcode allowed signing algorithms (e.g., `RS256` or `ES256`), cache IdP JWKS keys with `kid` lookup, and reject `alg=none`.
- **Single-Flight Refresh**: Wrap client-side token refresh in a mutex/promise queue so concurrent 401 responses share one `/oauth/token` call.
- **Sender-Constrained Tokens**: For high-security financial APIs (FAPI 2.0), bind tokens to the client's TLS certificate (mTLS `cnf.x5t#S256`) or ephemeral keypair (DPoP) so stolen Bearer tokens cannot be replayed from another host.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Require `code_challenge_method=S256` (PKCE) on all Authorization Code grants; disable Implicit and ROPC.
- [ ] Register exact `redirect_uri` values with no wildcards or open redirects.
- [ ] Generate and verify a cryptographic `state` parameter (and `nonce` for OIDC `id_token`) per login.
- [ ] Keep access token TTLs to 5–15 minutes and enable refresh token rotation with reuse detection.
- [ ] Validate `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `alg`, and `scope` on every Resource Server endpoint.
- [ ] Use a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) with `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookies for browser SPAs.

interviewProblems.title: OAuth2 Authorization Flows
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on OAuth2 Authorization Flows. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access without sharing user passwords, using distinct grant flows tailored to confidential backends, public SPAs/mobile apps, headless devices, and service-to-service workloads. Modern OAuth 2.1 deprecates the Implicit and Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flows in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Authorization Server applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Resource Server (API).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Resource Server (API) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Mandate PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) on the authorization server; the attacker cannot exchange the stolen `code` without the original `code_verifier`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) for any user-facing login and Client Credentials for machine-to-machine calls; never use Implicit or ROPC.
Avoid trap: Using `client_secret` inside a mobile app or SPA bundle—public clients cannot keep secrets, so any secret shipped in client code is compromised immediately.
Avoid trap: Confusing OAuth 2.0 (authorization) with OpenID Connect (authentication) and skipping `id_token` `nonce` and `aud` validation.
When to reach for it: Granting third-party or first-party web/mobile apps scoped, revocable access to user resources via `Authorization Code + PKCE`.
When to reach for it: Authenticating backend microservices or batch jobs to internal APIs via `Client Credentials` without a human user in the loop.

putItTogether.title: Putting Oauth2 Authorization Flows Together
putItTogether.summary: Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (`code_challenge_method=S256`) for any user-facing login and Client Credentials for machine-to-machine calls; never use Implicit or ROPC.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Oauth2 Authorization Flows before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Moving token exchange into an API Gateway BFF using Authorization Code + PKCE (`S256`) and issuing `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies eliminated token exposure in browser JS and cut token lifetime to 10 minutes with silent server-side refresh.
